scenario.title: The survey that arrived a week before the review
scenario.intro: An adoption survey from a seed-systems project in central Mexico lands on your desk a week before the quarterly evidence review. The same farmer appears three times under different spellings. One plot reports a maize yield far above anything seen in the area, another has a plot area of zero. Forty households have no answer to the adoption question. And every surveyed village sits on the main road, although the project wants to report adoption for the whole state. The number the review needs is in there somewhere. This module shows you how to get it out without inventing it.

objectives.text: Name the six quality dimensions (completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, representativeness) and match each problem in a dataset to the dimension it fails.
Design persistent identifiers and record-level provenance so that an observation can be found again and an institutional figure can be audited and recalculated.
Handle missing values and outliers by investigating and documenting them, rather than assuming zero or deleting them.
Judge whether a sample represents the population named in the claim and state the limits of the claim where it does not.
Set a validation cadence and assign quality roles: first-line checks at project level, periodic assurance at regional level, rules and remediation centrally.

beats.hook: A dataset with 2,000 rows looks solid. Then you notice the same farmer three times, a yield nobody has ever seen and forty blanks. How bad is it, exactly? The framework gives you six questions to answer that.

example.title: Fix the survey, watch the needle
example.prompt: Each dimension below has a problem from the Mexico adoption survey. Toggle the fix and watch the quality needle move. Notice which fix is not a cleaning step at all.

dimensions.label: Completeness
dimensions.problem: Forty households have no answer to the question on whether they planted the new variety.
dimensions.fix: Follow up the blanks where you can. Record the rest as unknown, not as zero, and note the gap.

dimensions.label: Accuracy
dimensions.problem: One plot reports a maize yield far above anything seen in the area. Another records a plot area of zero.
dimensions.fix: Range and consistency checks at entry flag these values. Each flagged value is investigated at source before anything is changed.

dimensions.label: Consistency
dimensions.problem: Plot area is recorded in hectares in one municipality and in a local unit in another, with no conversion noted.
dimensions.fix: Standardise formats and units using the shared data dictionary and controlled vocabularies.

dimensions.label: Timeliness
dimensions.problem: The dataset arrived three months after the season ended, after the review that needed it.
dimensions.fix: Run routine checks monthly and resolve exceptions close to collection, so the data are ready when decisions are made.

dimensions.label: Uniqueness
dimensions.problem: The same farmer appears three times under slightly different spellings of her name.
dimensions.fix: Use a persistent farmer identifier from the registry and apply the deduplication rule. Three rows become one.

dimensions.label: Representativeness
dimensions.problem: Every surveyed village sits on the main road. The claim is about smallholders across the whole state.
dimensions.fix: Compare the sample with the population in the claim. Extend coverage, or narrow the claim to the area sampled and say so.

bullets: Quality assurance validates, standardises, de-duplicates and documents provenance and quality.
Controls cover completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and representativeness.
A dataset can pass five dimensions and still fail the sixth. Check all six before you report.

lessons.title: Identifiers and provenance: can you find this observation again?

beats.hook: An investor asks how the figure of 1,240 adopting farmers was calculated. You have a total in a spreadsheet. Can you get from that total back to one farmer, one plot, one form?

example.title: One observation, from the field to the institutional figure
body: A seed-systems project in Mexico registers a farmer. She gets a persistent identifier: unique, stable, the same across this project, the next one and every year in between. Her plot gets one too. The framework asks for such identifiers for farmers, plots, households, organisations, trials and projects, because they link delivery to later uptake and outcomes and prevent double counting.

Her name would not do the job. It is spelled three ways in the dataset, two farmers in the municipality share it, and her phone number changed last year. An identifier assigned by the project in its own format is not enough either, because the next project would assign a new one and the link would be lost.

At the follow-up survey, the enumerator records her adoption answer against her identifier. The record carries its provenance: which form version, which date, which enumerator, which method. When the plot area is corrected a week later, the audit trail keeps the old value, the new value and the reason.

At the annual KPI run, the KPI engine calculates adoption from the eligible records with the approved method and reports coverage, uncertainty and method version. When the method improves next year, the figure can be recalculated from the same records. A total copied into a spreadsheet can be read. It cannot be audited, recalculated or reused.
That is the test for your own data: pick any figure in a report and try to reach one source record. If you cannot, the figure has no provenance.

bullets: Persistent identifiers are unique and stable for farmers, plots, households, organisations, trials and projects across projects and years.
Record-level provenance and an audit trail let institutional figures be audited and recalculated.
Names, phone numbers and project-specific numbers are not persistent identifiers.

lessons.title: Outliers, missingness and what to do before deleting anything

beats.hook: A plot reports a yield three times higher than its neighbours. Forty households left the adoption question blank. The quickest fix is delete one and zero the other. Both would be wrong.

example.title: Two values, one process
body: The outlier first. The framework does not give you a rule such as drop anything above a certain value. It gives you a process: outcome-level quality work addresses missing values, outliers, consistency and comparability, and the project team's role during implementation is to investigate anomalies. So you go back to the record. Was the plot area entered in the wrong unit? Did the enumerator measure a net plot or the whole field? Is this a trial plot that should not be in a farmer dataset at all? Each of those answers leads to a different, documented decision: correct the record, exclude it with a stated reason, or keep it because it is genuine.

If you simply deleted it, you would lose a true observation if it was real, and you would lose the chance to find a systematic error if it was not. Either way the audit trail would show a gap nobody can explain.

Now the blanks. A missing answer means you do not know whether that household planted the variety. Coding it as zero turns forty unknowns into forty confirmed non-adopters and silently lowers the adoption rate. Deleting the forty rows changes who is in your sample. The honest path is to follow up where you can, record the rest as missing, and report how many were missing and why.

Both decisions are exception handling, which the quality plan in the minimum package asks you to define. Write down what you flagged, what you found and what you decided. The next person to recalculate the figure, perhaps with a better method, needs to see it.

bullets: Outcome-level quality work addresses consistency, missing values, outliers and comparability.
Investigate a flagged value at source before you correct, exclude or keep it. Then document the decision.
A blank is an unknown, not a zero. Follow up, record it as missing and report the gap.

lessons.title: Representativeness: who is not in your sample?

beats.hook: Two thousand farmers answered the survey. That sounds like plenty. But every one of them lives within a short drive of the project office, and the report says the whole state.

example.title: The claim and the sample, side by side
body: Write the claim first: adoption of the new variety among smallholder maize farmers in the state. Now describe who was actually observed: farmers in the villages that host demonstration plots, all on the main road, surveyed in the dry season when remote households are hardest to reach. The gap between those two descriptions is the representativeness problem, and no amount of cleaning closes it. A big, clean sample of the wrong population is still the wrong population.

The framework's answer runs through its aggregation rules. At regional level, estimates define inclusion criteria, weight by area or representativeness, and report uncertainty bounds. Every institutional result is reported with its coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality. So the Focal Point has three honest options: extend coverage to the villages that were missed, narrow the claim to the area that was sampled, or report the state figure with its coverage and limits stated plainly.

There is a tempting fourth option: use satellite imagery to stand in for the villages you could not reach. The triangulation rule is strict here. A source strengthens a claim only when it measures the same construct, population, geography and period under compatible definitions. Satellite data do not replace ground observations where the KPI method requires direct measurement. They can calibrate, contextualise, stratify or upscale, under documented rules.
Representativeness is also an accountability question. The framework asks who benefits and who may be excluded. A sample that skips remote households cannot answer that.

bullets: Representativeness asks whether the observed sample matches the population named in the claim.
Results are reported with coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality. Narrow the claim or extend coverage; never quietly generalise.
A source strengthens a claim only if it measures the same construct, population, geography and period.

beats.hook: If the first quality check happens at endline, every error has had two years to spread into dashboards, reports and decisions. When should the first check happen instead?

example.title: A quality plan for the Mexico survey
body: The minimum package asks every project to leave inception with a quality plan: validation rules, first-line checks, deduplication, exception handling, provenance, audit trail and periodic MEAL assurance. None of these is left to end-of-project reporting. Here is what that means for the adoption survey.

At entry: the form, built from the KPI reference sheet, validates as data are collected. Automated completeness, range, consistency and duplicate checks raise quality flags. A plot area of zero and a yield far outside the expected range are flagged on the spot, not discovered three months later.

Continuous or monthly: the Focal Point works through the flags, investigates exceptions close to collection, corrects records and logs system issues. The typical outputs are quality flags, corrected records and a system issue log.
Quarterly or seasonal: the evidence review looks at implementation, reach and early uptake, and ends in a decision log of what changes, who acts and by when. Clean data make that meeting useful.

Annual: institutional KPIs are recomputed from eligible records, with coverage, uncertainty and evidence gaps reviewed. Because the records and their provenance were kept, a method improvement next year can be applied to this year's data. That is what re-analysis means. Frequency is adapted to seasonality and project risk, but the sequence is the same.

bullets: Continuous or monthly checks resolve exceptions close to collection. Outputs: quality flags, corrected records, system issue log.
The quality plan sets validation rules, first-line checks, deduplication, exception handling, provenance, audit trail and periodic assurance at inception.
Annual KPI runs recompute from eligible records, so kept records can be re-analysed as methods improve.

lessons.title: Roles: who checks what, and when

beats.hook: The duplicates are found. The outlier is explained. Who was supposed to do that, who follows up when it keeps happening, and who writes the rule so it stops happening everywhere?

example.title: Who does what?
example.prompt: Sort each quality task to the role the framework gives it. Think in layers: project, regional, core, infrastructure.

bins.label: Project MEAL Focal Point
bins.hint: Keeps source records and runs first-line checks close to implementation.

bins.label: Regional MEAL Lead
bins.hint: Follows up gaps across the regional portfolio and coaches Focal Points.

bins.label: Evidence Systems, Data Quality & Reporting Analyst
bins.hint: Core Layer. Defines the rules and monitors recurrent issues.

bins.label: Data Group
bins.hint: Owns the infrastructure that runs the checks.

cards.label: Run first-line quality checks on this month's adoption records
cards.why: First-line quality checks are a core responsibility of the Project MEAL Focal Point.

cards.label: Keep the project's source-level records up to date
cards.why: The Focal Point coordinates monitoring and keeps source-level records.

cards.label: Investigate the anomalies the system flagged this week
cards.why: During implementation, the project role is to maintain timely capture and investigate anomalies.

cards.label: Follow up recurring data-quality gaps with three project teams in the region
cards.why: Regional MEAL Leads follow up data-quality and reporting gaps with project teams, with support from Pillar B.

cards.label: Review KPI completeness across the regional dashboard
cards.why: Reviewing KPI completeness and performance through regional dashboards is a Regional MEAL Lead task.

cards.label: Coach a new Focal Point through an identifier problem
cards.why: Regional MEAL Leads coach Project MEAL Focal Points and guide their technical work.

cards.label: Define the deduplication and provenance rules for adoption records
cards.why: The analyst defines and implements validation, completeness, consistency, deduplication and provenance rules. Pillar B is accountable; the Data Group builds them into the system.

cards.label: Maintain the institutional MEAL data dictionary
cards.why: The data dictionary is maintained by the Evidence Systems, Data Quality and Reporting Analyst.

cards.label: Monitor recurrent data-quality issues across projects and support remediation
cards.why: Monitoring recurrent issues and supporting remediation sits with the analyst, who works with Regional MEAL Leads to resolve gaps.

cards.label: Run and maintain the infrastructure that executes the checks
cards.why: The Data Group owns the infrastructure. MEAL owns the content: indicators, data dictionary and quality rules.

cards.label: Software engineering for the MEAL data system
cards.why: Software engineering, advanced data science and geospatial processing remain with the Data Group and other technical functions.

bullets: Focal Points keep source records and run first-line checks. Regional MEAL Leads follow up gaps and are accountable for periodic QA.
The Evidence Systems, Data Quality and Reporting Analyst defines the rules and monitors recurrent issues centrally.
MEAL owns the quality rules. The Data Group owns the infrastructure that runs them.

frames.narration: A survey arrives from a seed-systems project in Mexico. Before you report anything from it, you need to know how good it is.
The framework checks six things: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and representativeness. This dataset has a problem on every one. The needle sits near the bottom.
Start with uniqueness. Three rows for one farmer become one, because the registry uses a persistent identifier, not a name. The needle moves.
Accuracy and consistency next. Range checks flag the impossible yield and the zero-area plot for investigation at source. Units are standardised with the data dictionary.
Completeness and timeliness. The blanks are followed up, not set to zero. Monthly checks will catch the next batch close to collection, not three months later.

scene.label: Gaps followed up, monthly checks set

frames.narration: The last segment does not move by cleaning. Only villages near the road were surveyed. You extend coverage, or you narrow the claim to the area you sampled and say so. Then the needle can move.

scene.label: Claim narrowed to the sampled area

frames.narration: Six dimensions, one dial. Clean what you can. Document what you cannot. Never report what you have not checked.

scene.title: Six dimensions, one dial
scene.subtitle: Clean what you can. Document what you cannot.

storyboards.title: Can you find this observation again?

frames.narration: Here is a report figure: 1,240 adopting farmers. Try to get from it back to one farmer, one plot, one form.

scene.title: 1,240 adopting farmers
scene.subtitle: Where did this number come from?

frames.narration: Follow one observation forward. A farmer is registered with a persistent identifier. Her adoption answer is recorded against it, with its provenance: form, date, enumerator, method. A later correction is logged in the audit trail. The KPI engine computes the figure from records like hers.
Now try the same walk with a name as the identifier. Three spellings, two farmers with the same name, a phone number that changed. The chain breaks at the first link.
With identifiers and provenance, a figure can be audited, recalculated when the method improves, and reused by the next project. Without them it is just a number.

scene.gap: Same number. Only one can be audited.

frames.narration: Three values from the Mexico survey. A yield far above every neighbour. A plot area of zero. Forty blank adoption answers. Each one tempts a quick fix.

The framework gives a process, not a threshold. A check flags the value. Someone investigates it at source. A decision follows: correct, exclude with a reason, or keep because it is genuine. Then it is documented in the audit trail.

steps.label: Investigate
steps.detail: Back to the form, the plot, the enumerator

steps.label: Decide
steps.detail: Correct, exclude with reason, or keep

frames.narration: Watch the two tempting fixes bounce. A blank tries to become a zero and comes back: it is unknown, so follow it up. The extreme yield tries the delete bin and comes back: investigate first.
Investigate before you delete. Record the unknown as unknown. Write down what you did, so the next analyst can see it.

scene.title: Investigate. Decide. Document.
scene.subtitle: A blank is not a zero. An outlier is not an error until you have checked.

storyboards.title: Who is not in your sample?

frames.narration: On the left, who was surveyed: two thousand farmers in roadside villages that host demonstration plots, reached in the dry season. On the right, who the claim is about: all smallholder maize farmers in the state. These are not the same population.

Three honest options. Extend coverage to the villages you missed. Narrow the claim to the area you sampled. Or report the wider figure with its coverage, uncertainty and limits stated plainly. Quietly generalising is not on the list.
A big sample of the wrong population is still the wrong population. Size does not fix representativeness. Coverage and honest limits do.

scene.title: Big is not representative
scene.subtitle: Compare the sample with the population in the claim.

frames.narration: Quality runs as a loop, not an event. Data are captured. The form validates at entry. Automated checks raise flags. Exceptions are resolved close to collection. The log records what changed.

steps.label: Capture
steps.detail: Form built from the KPI sheet

frames.narration: This loop runs continuously or monthly. Its outputs are quality flags, corrected records and a system issue log. Nothing waits for the annual report.

The monthly loop sits inside a wider cadence. Quarterly or seasonal reviews turn clean data into decisions. The annual run recomputes KPIs from eligible records and reviews coverage, uncertainty and gaps. Studies come at midterm, endline or when a trigger fires.
Because the records and their provenance are kept, this year's figure can be recalculated next year with a better method. Check monthly. Re-analyse annually.

scene.title: Check monthly. Re-analyse annually.
scene.subtitle: Exceptions resolved close to collection, never at endline.

frames.narration: Quality has four layers. The Focal Point keeps source records and runs first-line checks. The Regional MEAL Lead follows up gaps across projects. The Evidence Systems analyst writes the rules and watches recurrent issues. The Data Group runs the infrastructure.

layers.label: Evidence Systems, Data Quality & Reporting Analyst
Regional MEAL Lead
layers.detail: Follow-up of gaps, coaching, periodic QA

frames.narration: Watch four tasks find their owner. First-line checks try the Data Group and bounce back to the Focal Point. Follow-up across the region lands with the Regional Lead. The deduplication rule goes to the analyst. The server goes to the Data Group.
Central standards, distributed implementation, institutional integration. Each task has one owner, and the handoffs are explicit.

scene.title: One owner per task
scene.subtitle: Rules centrally. Checks at the project. Follow-up in the region.

misconceptions.description: You treated a blank or missing value as a confirmed zero. A blank means you do not know; coding it as zero invents an observation and hides the gap.
You removed or capped an unusual value without investigating its cause. An outlier is not an error until you have checked the record at source and documented the decision.
You assumed that a large or clean sample can speak for the whole population in the claim. Size does not fix who was left out.
You used a name, phone number or project-specific number to link records. The framework asks for identifiers that are unique and stable across projects and years.
You accepted a reported total, screenshot or summary as sufficient. Without record-level provenance and an audit trail, a figure cannot be audited or recalculated.
You placed quality checks at endline or at the annual report. The cadence runs continuous or monthly checks, with exceptions resolved close to collection.
You handed first-line quality work to central MEAL or the Data Group. Project teams run first-line checks and keep source records; central roles set rules and follow up.

questions.question: In an adoption dataset from a seed-systems project in Mexico, the same farmer appears three times under slightly different spellings. Which quality dimension is failing?

options.text: Timeliness
Uniqueness
Representativeness
Completeness

questions.explanation: Uniqueness is the control that catches the same entity recorded more than once, and quality assurance de-duplicates records. Completeness is about missing values, not repeated ones.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Quality Assurance row of the five functions table and list its six controls.

questions.question: Plot area is recorded in hectares in one municipality and in a local unit in another, with no conversion noted. Which dimension does this fail?

options.text: Consistency
Uniqueness
Timeliness
Representativeness

questions.explanation: Mixed formats and units are a consistency problem, which quality assurance addresses by standardising. Uniqueness concerns duplicate records, not differing units.
questions.reviewTip: Match each of the six controls to one concrete problem in a dataset you know.

questions.question: What does the framework require of identifiers for farmers, plots, households, organisations, trials and projects?

options.text: Renewed each year so old records are not confused with new ones
Assigned by each project in whatever format suits its forms
Unique and stable across projects and years
Built from the participant's name and village of residence

questions.explanation: Persistent identifiers are unique, stable IDs that hold across projects and years, so delivery can be linked to later uptake and double counting is prevented. An identifier that changes each year or each project breaks that link.
questions.reviewTip: Read the persistent identifiers row of the nine functionalities.

questions.question: Why does the framework keep the underlying records and their provenance, rather than only the reported totals?

options.text: So that project reports can be shortened to a single total
So that results can be recalculated, audited and reused as methods improve
So that each investor can keep its own copy of the dataset
So that enumerators can be paid per record collected

questions.explanation: The MEAL data system keeps the underlying records and their provenance so institutional results can be recalculated, audited and reused as methods improve. A total on its own supports none of that.
questions.reviewTip: Read the paragraph after the five functions table about what the data system keeps.

questions.question: Forty households left the question on planting the new variety blank. What should the team do?

options.text: Record them as non-adopters so that the total can be reported on time
Drop the forty households from every analysis of the dataset
Treat the answer as unknown, follow up where possible and document the gap
Replace each blank with the most common answer in the district

questions.explanation: Outcome-level quality work addresses missing values, and a blank is an unknown, not a zero. Recording them as non-adopters invents forty observations and lowers the adoption rate without evidence.
questions.reviewTip: Separate the question of what the value is from the question of how to report that you do not know it.

questions.question: A smallholder maize plot shows a yield several times higher than any other plot in the dataset. What is the first step?

options.text: Delete the record so that it cannot distort the average
Investigate the record: check plot area, units and the source form
Keep it unchanged and publish the average without comment
Cap the value at the next highest plot in the dataset

questions.explanation: During implementation, the project role is to investigate anomalies, and quality work addresses outliers before comparison. Deleting or capping without checking loses a genuine observation if it was real and hides a systematic error if it was not.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the project role in Phase 5 of the lifecycle table.

questions.question: Which question tests the representativeness of a dataset?

options.text: Does the sample match the population the claim is about?
Are all the recorded values within the permitted range?
Were the records submitted before the review meeting?
Is each farmer counted exactly once in the dataset?

questions.explanation: Representativeness is about whether the observed units can stand for the population named in the claim. The other questions test accuracy, timeliness and uniqueness.
questions.reviewTip: Write the claim and the sample description side by side and look for the gap.

questions.question: A team surveyed 2,000 farmers along the main road and wants to report adoption for the whole state. What does the framework expect?

options.text: Report the state figure, because 2,000 is a large sample
Report with coverage and limits stated, or narrow the claim to the area sampled
Discard the survey, because it cannot be used for anything
Double the sample size along the same road next season

questions.explanation: Results are reported with their coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality, and aggregation defines inclusion criteria and weights by representativeness. A larger sample of the same roadside villages does not change who is missing.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

questions.reviewTip: Read how institutional values are reported in 3.3 and the regional row of the yield table in 3.2.

questions.question: What are the typical outputs of the continuous or monthly cadence?

options.text: Evaluation findings and an updated impact narrative
A portfolio dashboard and an evidence-gap register
A decision log of what changes, who acts and by when
Quality flags, corrected records and a system issue log

questions.explanation: The continuous or monthly row of the cadence table lists quality flags, corrected records and a system issue log. The decision log belongs to the quarterly review and the dashboard and gap register to the annual run.
questions.reviewTip: Read the four rows of the cadence table and their typical outputs.

questions.question: Data-quality gaps keep appearing in several projects in one region. Who follows them up with the project teams?

options.text: The Regional MEAL Lead, with support from Pillar B
The MEAL Group Lead, in person with each project
The Data Group, through the system issue log
The Evaluation and Research Specialist

questions.explanation: Regional MEAL Leads follow up data-quality and reporting gaps with project teams, supported by Pillar B. The Group Lead reviews portfolio-level evidence quality but does not chase individual project gaps.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Regional MEAL Lead responsibilities in 5.8.

questions.question: A clean, complete adoption dataset reaches the Focal Point three months after the season, after the review that needed it. Which dimension failed?

options.text: Accuracy
Completeness
Uniqueness
Timeliness

questions.explanation: Timeliness is one of the six quality controls, and data that arrive after the decision they were meant to inform fail it. Completeness and accuracy were fine here; the problem was when the data arrived.
questions.reviewTip: Check each dataset against all six controls, not only the ones that are easy to see.

questions.question: A dataset has every row filled, no duplicates, values in range and arrived on time. It was collected only in villages near the project office. What can you say about its quality?

options.text: It passes all six quality dimensions
It fails completeness because some villages are absent
It fails uniqueness because villages are repeated
It passes five dimensions and fails representativeness

questions.explanation: Representativeness is a separate control: a dataset can be complete, accurate, consistent, timely and unique and still not stand for the population in the claim. Completeness concerns missing values in the records collected, not villages that were never sampled.
questions.reviewTip: Keep representativeness as its own check, after the other five pass.

questions.question: Which statement about the six quality dimensions is correct?

options.text: Passing one dimension does not guarantee passing the others
A large dataset passes representativeness automatically
Duplicate records are a completeness problem
Timeliness only matters at endline reporting

questions.explanation: The six controls are separate, so a dataset must be checked against each one. Duplicates are a uniqueness problem, size does not settle representativeness, and timeliness matters whenever a decision depends on the data.
questions.reviewTip: Apply the six controls one by one to a dataset you have handled recently.

questions.question: Two projects in the same region record the same farmer. One uses her name, the other a phone number that changed last year. What does the framework ask for instead?

options.text: A name-plus-village key agreed between the two projects
A separate total from each project, added together
A persistent, unique identifier shared across projects and years
A note in each report that overlap between them is possible

questions.explanation: Persistent identifiers are unique and stable across projects and years, which is what links delivery to later uptake and prevents double counting. A name-plus-village key still breaks on spelling, namesakes and moves.
questions.reviewTip: Read why MEAL needs persistent identifiers in the 4.1 table.

questions.question: An investor asks how the figure of 1,240 adopting farmers was calculated. The team has only the total in a spreadsheet. What is missing?

options.text: A larger sample of farmers drawn from the same districts
A signed approval of the total from the project lead
Record-level provenance and an audit trail linking the figure to source records
A more recent dashboard export showing the same total

questions.explanation: The system keeps record-level provenance and an audit trail so that institutional figures can be audited and recalculated. A signature or a dashboard export vouches for the number without showing where it came from.
questions.reviewTip: Pick a figure from your last report and try to reach one source record from it.

questions.question: The KPI Toolbox updates the method for an adoption indicator. Which project can rerun last year's figure under the new method?

options.text: The one that kept its investor report as a signed PDF
The one that kept the reported total and the enumerator names
The one that kept a monthly screenshot of its dashboard
The one that kept the underlying records with their provenance

questions.explanation: The data system keeps underlying records and their provenance precisely so results can be recalculated as methods improve, and the KPI engine reports the method version used. Totals, PDFs and screenshots cannot be recomputed.
questions.reviewTip: Read the KPI engine row in 4.1 alongside the paragraph on the data system in 2.5.

questions.question: A field officer proposes filling every blank yield cell with zero so that the dataset is complete. What is wrong with this?

options.text: A blank is an unknown value, so coding it as zero invents an observation and hides the gap
Nothing is wrong, because a blank and a zero mean the same thing in a survey
The blanks should be filled with the district mean instead of with zero
Only the Data Group is allowed to fill blank cells in a project dataset

questions.explanation: Missing values are a quality issue to be addressed, not erased: a zero yield is a measured result, a blank is the absence of one. Filling with a mean also invents data; the honest record says the value is missing and why.
questions.reviewTip: Report how many values are missing and why, rather than making the gap disappear.

questions.question: After investigation, an unusually high yield turns out to be a genuine, correctly measured observation. What should happen to it?

options.text: Delete it, because it will distort the comparison across projects
Replace it with the sample median to keep the average stable
Keep it, record the investigation, and consider its effect on comparability
Move it to a separate dataset so that it is not reported at all

questions.explanation: A verified observation is evidence; outcome-level quality work handles outliers and comparability by investigating and documenting, not by removing what is true. Deleting or replacing it would falsify the record and leave an unexplained gap in the audit trail.
questions.reviewTip: Decide what to do with a flagged value only after you know its cause.

questions.question: A Focal Point notes that 12 records were excluded as duplicates and 3 extreme values were kept after verification. Why does the framework want this written down?

options.text: So the audit trail shows what changed and why, and the figure can be recalculated
So the enumerators responsible for the errors can be identified
So the dataset looks cleaner when it is shared with investors
So the extreme values can be deleted later without a new review

questions.explanation: The quality plan includes exception handling, provenance and an audit trail, and the data system keeps record-level provenance so figures can be audited and recalculated. Documentation is for traceability, not for blame or appearance.
questions.reviewTip: Read element 5 of the minimum package, the quality plan.

questions.question: A project reports adoption for smallholders across the state from a sample drawn only from villages that host demonstration plots. What should the Focal Point do first?

options.text: Increase the sample within the same demonstration villages
Report the state figure, since the sample is large and clean
Replace the survey with satellite imagery of the whole state
Compare the sampled villages with the population in the claim and narrow or qualify the claim

questions.explanation: Representativeness asks whether the observed farms can support the intended claim, and results are reported with their coverage and limits. More farmers from the same villages do not change who was left out, and satellite data cannot replace required ground observations.
questions.reviewTip: Write down the population in the claim before you look at the sample.

questions.question: A team wants satellite imagery to stand in for the villages it could not reach in its adoption survey. What does the triangulation rule say?

options.text: Satellite data can replace the missing ground observations whenever field coverage is incomplete
Satellite data help only if they measure the same construct, population, geography and period, under documented rules
Satellite data are never a valid source for any adoption indicator at any measurement level
Satellite data count as direct observations once they have been calibrated once

questions.explanation: A source strengthens a claim only when it measures the same construct, population, geography and period under compatible definitions, and satellite data do not replace ground observations where the KPI method requires direct measurement. They can calibrate, contextualise, stratify or upscale under documented rules.
questions.reviewTip: Read the triangulation rule at the end of section 2.6.

questions.question: A project plans to check data quality once, at endline, just before the final report. What does the operating cadence say?

options.text: That is sufficient if the endline study is well resourced
Checks run continuously or monthly, with exceptions resolved close to collection
Checks happen only during the annual institutional KPI run
Checks are the Data Group's job once collection has ended

questions.explanation: The cadence table places routine data-quality checks in the continuous or monthly row, with exceptions resolved close to collection. An endline-only check lets errors spread into every dashboard and decision before anyone sees them.
questions.reviewTip: Read the first row of the cadence table and the quality plan element in 5.4.

questions.question: Who runs first-line quality checks on routine activity and output data, and who is accountable for periodic QA and completeness checks?

options.text: Data Group for first-line checks; Core Layer for periodic QA
Regional MEAL Lead for first-line checks; Focal Point for periodic QA
Focal Point for first-line checks; Regional MEAL Lead accountable for periodic QA
Core Layer for both first-line checks and periodic QA

questions.explanation: In the RACI, the Focal Point is responsible for routine collection and first-line QA, and the Regional MEAL Lead is accountable for periodic QA and completeness checks, with Pillar B consulted. Central roles set rules and follow up; they do not run first-line checks.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the Phase 5 rows of the RACI matrix.

questions.question: Who owns the content of the quality rules (validation, deduplication, provenance), and who owns the infrastructure that runs them?

options.text: The Data Group owns both the rules and the infrastructure
Each project owns its own rules and its own infrastructure
The Regional MEAL Lead owns both for the regional portfolio
MEAL owns the rules; the Data Group owns the infrastructure

questions.explanation: The design principles split responsibility: the Data Group owns the infrastructure and the MEAL team owns the content, meaning indicators, data dictionary and quality rules. Within MEAL, the Evidence Systems, Data Quality and Reporting Analyst defines and implements those rules.
questions.reviewTip: Read the last sentence of 4.2 and the analyst's responsibilities in 5.8.

glossaryAdditions.definition: The record-level log of what changed in a dataset, when, by whom and why, kept so that institutional figures can be audited and recalculated.
Element of the minimum MEAL package that sets validation rules, first-line checks, deduplication, exception handling, provenance, audit trail and periodic MEAL assurance for a project.
The routine checks run by the Project MEAL Focal Point and project team on source-level records, close to collection, before periodic assurance by regional and central MEAL.
